function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository (or generate via the helper functions if you prefer).  
After adding them, just stage, commit and push as usual.

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile

```Dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image – it’s small and contains everything we need
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json & package-lock.json first so npm install can be cached
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is the smallest official Node image that still contains the full Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The `WORKDIR` keeps the container tidy and makes the `CMD` easier to read.  

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or any name you like) with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3          # Adjust the number of pods you want
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to ClusterIP/NodePort if you don’t have an external LB
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80           # Port exposed to the cluster
    targetPort: 3000   # Port your container listens on
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 3 replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the app via a LoadBalancer (use `ClusterIP` if you’re only testing locally).  
> * Uses environment variable `NODE_ENV=production` – you can add more env vars here if needed.

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: |
          k8s/deployment.yaml
        images: |
          ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # Base64‑encoded kubeconfig
```

### What you’ll need in **GitHub Secrets**

| Secret | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` | Your Docker Hub username |
| `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` | A Docker Hub access token (not your password) |
| `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` | Base64‑encoded kubeconfig for the cluster you’re deploying to |

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Builds the Docker image on every push to `main`.  
> * Pushes the image to Docker Hub.  
> * Deploys the new image to your Kubernetes cluster using the `azure/k8s-deploy` action (works with any cluster that accepts a kubeconfig).  

---

## 4️⃣ Add, Commit & Push

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo (if you haven’t already)
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# 2. Create the files above (or copy/paste them into the repo)

# 3. Stage the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml

# 4. Commit with a meaningful message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI/CD workflow"

# 5. Push to the remote
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger, build the Docker image, push it to Docker Hub, and deploy it to your Kubernetes cluster.

---

### Quick Checklist

- [ ] Dockerfile is in the repo root.  
- [ ] Kubernetes YAML is under `k8s/` (or wherever you prefer).  
- [ ] GitHub Actions workflow is under `.github/workflows/`.  
- [ ] All required secrets are added to the repo settings.  
- [ ] You have a running Kubernetes cluster accessible via a kubeconfig.  

That’s it! 🎉 If you hit any snags (e.g., authentication errors, missing secrets), let me know and I’ll help troubleshoot.
